title: Rank-Selective Optical Tomography of Higher-Wave Altermagnetism
authors: Meysam Bagheri Tagani, Carmine Autieri, Sahar Izadi Vishkayi
abstract: Identifying the spatial rank of higher-wave altermagnetic order optically is challenging because local electric-dipole response does not uniquely resolve distinct continuum harmonics. We show that finite photon momentum turns one-photon spin-resolved absorption into a rank-selective tomography. For the planar $|m|=\ell$ sector of an even-parity $\ell$-wave component, a joint Fourier projection in polarization and momentum angle isolates $\mathcal T_\ell\proptoη_\ell q^{\ell-2}$, yielding the hierarchy $d:q^0$, $g:q^2$, and $i:q^4$; phase changes track rotations of the selected magnetic harmonic. A Ward-consistent finite-$q$ microscopic calculation reproduces these powers without imposing them. Although discrete crystal symmetry can generate lower-order local aliases, they are orthogonal to the selected momentum harmonic and cannot contaminate it below $q^{\ell-2}$. In MnTe, whose nonrelativistic parent order is three-dimensional $g$ wave while spin--orbit coupling lowers the exact relativistic spin-momentum-locking symmetry, first-principles calculations show that more than $99.9\%$ of the Fourier power of the Néel-projected $A$-region spin-energy contrast remains in the parent $g$-wave-derived $m=3$ harmonic. Structured near fields place the required momentum window within experimental reach.
summary: This work presents a novel optical technique to determine the spatial rank of higher-wave magnetic order in altermagnets. By measuring the absorption spectrum using finite photon momentum, the authors show that a joint Fourier projection isolates the magnetic harmonic's rank via a characteristic power-law dependence on momentum. This method provides a robust diagnostic tool for characterizing complex magnetic textures in materials like MnTe.
main_problem: The primary challenge is optically identifying the spatial rank of higher-wave altermagnetism because local electric-dipole response cannot uniquely resolve distinct continuum harmonics.
main_result: By utilizing finite photon momentum and a joint Fourier projection, the spatial rank ($\ell$) can be selectively isolated, yielding a power law scaling of $|T_\ell| \propto q^{\ell-2}$.
method: The authors derive a rank-matching rule and employ a joint Fourier projection in polarization and momentum angle, which is verified by a Ward-consistent finite-q microscopic calculation.
model_or_system: The study focuses on altermagnetic materials exhibiting higher-wave order (d-, g-, or i-wave), using MnTe as a testbed. The analysis involves calculating the joint Fourier projection of the spin-resolved absorption rate.
key_observables: The joint Fourier projection $T_\ell(q, \omega)$, which exhibits a power law scaling $|T_\ell| \propto q^{\ell-2}$ corresponding to the rank $\ell$.
important_parameters: The photon momentum $q$ is crucial for achieving rank selectivity; the scaling exponent is $\ell-2$.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the finite photon momentum supplies the necessary missing spatial rank information, and the joint projection successfully filters out lower-order crystalline aliases.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the rank-matching principle via joint angular tomography ($d: q^0, g: q^2, i: q^4$) and show that the parent $g$-wave component remains strongly encoded in MnTe despite strong SOC effects.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical necessity of finite photon momentum for rank-selective tomography, derives the projection formula, and then applies this method to first-principles calculations on MnTe to confirm the persistence of the higher-wave magnetic texture.
why_interesting: The technique of using momentum-resolved spectroscopy to extract higher-order spatial harmonics is a powerful, non-linear optical diagnostic tool applicable to complex magnetic order parameters, bridging condensed matter theory with advanced quantum optics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Rank-selective optical tomography. Panel (a) shows representative two-dimensional continuum basis functions used to illustrate the rank-matching principle; material-specific three-dimensional g-wave harmonics may have a different in-plane winding. (b) Linear polarization supplies spatial rank two, while photon momentum supplies the remaining rank, giving d : q0, g : q2, and i : q4. (c) Field-free finite-q geometry. (d) A joint angular projection isolates Tℓ∝ηℓqℓ−2; the small-q scaling of its magnitude identifies the spatial-dispersion order, while phase changes track the relative orientation of the magnetic harmonic.

FIG. 2. Microscopic rank hierarchy and crystalline protection. (a) The projected response scales as q0, q2, and q4 for d-, g-, and i-wave order. (b) Rotating the texture produces phase windings 2, 4, and 6. (c) Rank bookkeeping for the g-wave channel and its C6 local alias. (d) The local mθ = 2 linear-polarization harmonic F2(q = 0) is linear in the hexagonal anisotropy β6. (e) Despite this alias, the projected T4 retains its q2 onset. Parameters and convergence tests are given in the SM.
